nameStory: This maple gets its name from the Tatar peoples of southern Russia, reflecting its vast natural range across central and southeastern Europe into temperate Asia. You might also see it spelled "Tartar" or "Tartarian" maple in older books, though these are considered misspellings of the original name honoring the Tatar culture.
description: Tatarian maple is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that's quite rare in New England, with only a couple recorded sightings. It typically grows 15-20 feet tall with a rounded, bushy crown that's often wider than it is tall. Like other maples, it produces the classic winged seeds (called samaras) that helicopter down in fall, but its leaves and overall appearance can look quite different from our familiar native maples.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves are the real surprise - unlike most maples, they're often unlobed or have just shallow lobes, looking almost oval with serrated edges. They feel smooth and papery, turning yellow to reddish in fall.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, creamy-white flowers appear in upright clusters after the leaves emerge in spring. They have a sweet, subtle fragrance and attract various small pollinators.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The winged seeds are reddish-pink when young, maturing to brown, and hang in dense clusters. They're smaller than sugar maple seeds with wings that form a narrow V-shape.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young, developing shallow furrows with age. The bark feels firm and doesn't peel like some other small maples.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often multi-stemmed with a dense, rounded crown. Branches tend to be somewhat drooping, giving it a softer appearance than the upright native maples.

habitat: In New England, Tatarian maple is extremely rare and likely found only in cultivated settings like botanical gardens, parks, or as landscape plantings. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. Given its rarity here, any sighting would be noteworthy and worth documenting.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in late April to early May, followed by clusters of small, fragrant white flowers. The fresh green foliage looks surprisingly un-maple-like to most observers.
seasonality.summer: Dense green foliage provides good shade, while the developing seed clusters turn from green to pinkish-red. The leaves maintain their smooth, oval appearance through the hot months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange-red before dropping. The mature seeds turn brown and eventually fall, though some may persist into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the rounded, somewhat drooping structure. Small buds and any remaining seed clusters can help with identification, along with the smooth gray bark.

funFact: This maple is so rare in New England that finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure - with only 2 recorded observations in the entire region, you'd be more likely to spot a celebrity than this elusive tree!
confusionNotes: The biggest confusion comes from expecting it to look like a "typical" maple - the often unlobed leaves can make people think it's not a maple at all! The winged seeds are the giveaway that it's definitely in the maple family, even when the leaves look more like a cherry or elm.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be thrown off by the various spellings you might encounter - "Tartar" and "Tartarian" maple are older, incorrect spellings that still appear in some references. The correct name honors the Tatar people and culture of the tree's native range.
compareHints: Unlike our common native maples with their distinctly lobed leaves, Tatarian maple often has simple, oval leaves with just shallow lobes or none at all. While Norway and sugar maples have large, deeply-cut leaves, and red maples have three-lobed leaves, Tatarian maple's foliage looks almost like it belongs on a different type of tree entirely. The telltale maple family trait is those unmistakable winged seeds that helicopter down in autumn.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop.
Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England.
